routes.description: Establish Christian revelation as the necessary precondition for truth, logic, knowledge, induction, evidence, and reasonable belief in God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the Christian God supplies the required foundation for intelligibility and that denying this foundation leaves the con account unable to justify its own reasoning.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's truth and necessary epistemic role to the conclusion that belief in the Christian God is reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective truth and knowledge require conformity to an absolute divine mind.
Establish that logical absolutes reflect God's thinking and cannot be grounded by autonomous naturalistic cognition.
Establish divine revelation as a certainty-conferring source available to human knowers.
Establish that nonrevelatory attempts to justify induction depend circularly on induction itself.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Christian revelation from competing religious authorities through internal consistency tests.
Clarify that Christianity functions as the argument's starting precondition rather than as an inference from generic absolutes.

routes.description: Defend fallibilist, evidence-responsive inquiry as sufficient for reasonable belief while requiring support for Christianity's claimed epistemic necessity.
routes.successCriteria: Show that reasonableness does not require absolute certainty, that logic and experience support provisional knowledge, and that revelation and Christian exclusivity require independent demonstration.

motionBridge.description: Connect justified fallibilist inquiry and unmet theistic evidential burdens to withholding belief in God as presently unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Define reasonable belief by valid inference and supported premises rather than by absolute certainty.
Ground inquiry in logical absolutes, shared experience, and appropriately limited confidence without adding God.
Require demonstration that Christianity uniquely accounts for logic, truth, and knowledge rather than merely asserting it.
Require a reliable mechanism connecting purported divine revelation to accurate human knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend induction as probabilistic justification without recasting it as deductive certainty.
Use disagreement among religious claims to require a truth-tracking method for selecting among revelations.

sections.title: Reasonableness, truth, and the burden of belief
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the motion-level standard and determines whether truth itself establishes reasonable theistic belief or whether supported premises and valid inference remain necessary.

sections.title: Objective reality, certainty, and radical skepticism
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of access to reality determine whether uncertainty about ultimate reality defeats secular knowledge or permits inquiry from minimal fallibilist commitments.

sections.title: The foundation and intelligibility of logic
sections.rationale: Accounting for logical absolutes is a central burden because both routes rely on logic while disputing whether its intelligibility requires the Christian God.

sections.title: Revelation, reliability, and rival religious claims
sections.rationale: The reliability and distinctiveness of Christian revelation govern whether it can bridge divine omniscience to human certainty and distinguish Christianity from competing authorities.

sections.title: Induction and the direction of the transcendental argument
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether probabilistic prediction can be rational without revelation and clarifies whether Christianity is established from shared premises or installed as the necessary starting point.

routes.description: Defend Christianity by connecting its account of sin and redemption to coherent explanations of suffering, divine judgment, biblical law, equality, and disputed Pauline instructions.
routes.successCriteria: Christianity's claims withstand the objections if its teachings on forgiveness and judgment remain morally coherent and the contested scriptural passages admit interpretations consistent with human dignity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account of salvation and divine goodness remains coherent across the principal moral and textual objections.

centralBridges.description: Explain how sin, Christ's sacrifice, forgiveness, judgment, and promised restoration form a coherent account of the human condition.
Reconcile divine jealousy, anger, and judgment with protective love, mercy, grace, and moral opposition to evil.
Interpret slavery regulations and restrictions on women without treating them as universal endorsements of ownership or subordination.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect disputed provisions to broader biblical themes of equal dignity, liberation, inclusion, and spiritual equality.
Use textual and congregational context to distinguish situational regulation from universal moral prescription.

routes.description: Challenge Christianity by presenting psychological alternatives to its consoling claims and testing divine goodness against troubling biblical portrayals, laws, and institutional restrictions.
routes.successCriteria: The skeptical critique satisfies its burden if central Christian defenses fail to reconcile the cited moral and textual difficulties with claims of divine goodness and scriptural authority.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cited Christian claims face unresolved explanatory, moral, or scriptural tensions substantial enough to defeat their proposed coherence.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Christianity's existential usefulness supplies a plausible psychological explanation distinct from the truth of its claims.
Test whether biblical portrayals of jealousy, violence, mutability, mercy, and love describe a morally consistent divine character.
Show that specific slavery provisions authorize ownership or coercion not explained merely as humane regulation of an existing practice.
Show that explicit Pauline restrictions create a moral problem not resolved by broader claims about Christian equality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use the rule separating a freed man from his family to test the claimed protective or transitional purpose of slavery legislation.
Test abolitionist use of spiritual-unity language against the parallel persistence of earthly male and female distinctions.

sections.title: Redemption, suffering, and explanatory origin
sections.rationale: This issue establishes Christianity's account of sin, forgiveness, suffering, judgment, and restoration while testing whether its existential appeal supports truth or an alternative psychological origin.

sections.title: Divine anger, love, and scriptural consistency
sections.rationale: The coherence of divine goodness depends on whether the Bible's depictions of jealousy, anger, violence, mercy, and love can describe one morally consistent divine character.

sections.title: Slavery law, regulation, and coercion
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether biblical slavery provisions merely constrain wrongdoing in a fallen society or instead authorize ownership and avoidable coercion contrary to divine justice.

sections.title: Canonical equality and earthly slavery
sections.rationale: The broader scriptural case against slavery turns on whether creation, liberation, inclusion, and unity in Christ condemn earthly slavery or describe equality compatible with continuing social distinctions.

sections.title: Women teaching and speaking in church
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether New Testament evidence supports women's participation in teaching and worship or imposes a general rule of silence and subordination.

routes.description: Establish resurrection as a plausible cumulative explanation of the early appearances, unexpected resurrection belief, subsequent Christian expansion, and continuing visions.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the historical lines jointly fit Jesus's resurrection and continuing agency more specifically than the proposed ordinary or comparative explanations.

motionBridge.description: The combined historical lines must make Jesus's resurrection a plausible explanation of the motion's specified phenomena.

centralBridges.description: Early individual and group appearance traditions must provide positive evidence that Jesus was encountered alive after death.
The immediate claim of an individually resurrected Messiah must require explanation beyond available Jewish postmortem categories.
Christianity's expansion must connect specifically to the mission and continuing agency attributed to the risen Jesus.
Later cross-cultural Jesus visions must constitute an additional phenomenon consistent with his continuing activity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: No single evidential line must bear the entire case; the lines must retain cumulative relevance when considered together.
Christian appearance and vision reports must be distinguishable from proposed parallels by their attestation, unexpectedness, or cross-cultural pattern.

routes.description: Account for the appearance beliefs, resurrection interpretation, Christian expansion, and later visions without treating a physical resurrection as the probable historical explanation.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source limitations, ordinary experiential mechanisms, cultural interpretation, religious growth, and comparative cases block the resurrection inference.

motionBridge.description: The available historical evidence must remain insufficient to prefer a unique physical resurrection over ordinary or historically comparable explanations.

centralBridges.description: The appearance evidence must be constrained by indirect testimony, sparse descriptions, and uncertainty about the reported witnesses.
Experiences and apocalyptic Jewish beliefs must supply a nonresurrection route to sincere claims that Jesus had been raised.
Religious expansion and fulfilled-mission claims must not establish what happened physically to Jesus's body.
Later Jesus dreams and visions must remain explainable through phenomena also reported in other religious traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical inference must compare probabilities without assuming either that miracles are impossible or that testimony establishes them.
Standards applied to Christian testimony must also be applied to Mormon, Marian, and ancient appearance traditions.

sections.title: Early appearance testimony and comparative attestation
sections.rationale: The quality, number, and comparative force of the earliest reported witnesses form the principal evidential link between postmortem experiences and resurrection.

sections.title: Unexpected messianic claim and Jewish interpretive categories
sections.rationale: The origin of belief in an already resurrected Messiah determines whether the claim itself points beyond ordinary experience or follows from available cultural interpretation.

sections.title: Cumulative fit and historical probability
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether several converging facts can make resurrection plausible despite the methodological difficulty of inferring a singular physical event.

sections.title: Christian expansion and the worldwide mission claim
sections.rationale: Christianity's historical reach matters only if its scale or fulfillment of an attributed mission bears specifically on resurrection rather than merely recording successful belief.

sections.title: Later visions and cross-religious parallels
sections.rationale: Post-apostolic dreams and visions provide an additional proposed evidential line whose relevance depends on whether they indicate continuing agency or generic religious experience.

routes.description: Establish a necessary sustaining source of dependent being and show that classical divine attributes remain coherent with creation, temporality, freedom, evil, and revelation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if dependent reality requires a divine ground and the principal coherence and evidential objections do not undermine identifying that ground with classical God.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary explanatory ground of dependent reality to the existence of the God affirmed by classical theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that changes from potency to act and essentially ordered causes require a presently sustaining foundational actuality.
Reconcile pure actuality with divine freedom, immutable knowledge, and creaturely temporal succession.
Explain divine goodness, creation, and permitted evil without treating God as one finite moral agent among others.
Explain why loving divine self-disclosure may be gradual and non-coercive despite nonbelief and religious disagreement.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that natural reason can reach truths about God despite uneven access and intellectual difficulty.
Ground practical norms in the natures, ends, and flourishing of beings.

routes.description: Undermine classical theism by challenging its cosmological inference and identifying conflicts between its divine attributes and freedom, time, evil, and loving disclosure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive inference to classical God remains unsupported or if central divine attributes conflict with temporal reality, suffering, freedom, or widespread nonbelief.

motionBridge.description: Show that the evidence and coherence objections jointly favor denial of the classical-theist God specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Challenge termination, uniqueness, sustaining causation, and the inference from a first cause to the attributes of classical God.
Show that pure actuality and immutability conflict with alternative possibilities and knowledge of changing temporal truths.
Establish that apparently gratuitous evolutionary suffering is more expected without a perfectly good providential creator.
Show that perfect divine love is difficult to reconcile with nonresistant nonbelief and extensive religious disagreement.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify the simplicity, immutability, timelessness, impassibility, freedom, and goodness claims under examination.
Provide objective moral and epistemic grounds for moving from apparently needless suffering to an evidential objection.

sections.title: Dependence, Causal Series, and Sustaining Being
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal positive inference from observed dependence to a foundational cause and the objections to termination and continuous sustaining causation.

sections.title: Pure Actuality and Divine Freedom
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the classical account of pure actuality can preserve the traditional claim that creation is a perfectly free divine act.

sections.title: Eternity, Immutability, and Changing Knowledge
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether an immutable and purely actual God can know a world whose temporally indexed truths and existing subjects change.

sections.title: Evolutionary Evil and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This issue tests the evidential force of extensive animal suffering and the competing accounts of creation, moral evaluation, divine goodness, and permitted evil.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Revelation, and Religious Disagreement
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether difficult access to belief and persistent religious diversity are compatible with a perfectly loving God seeking relationship with finite persons.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning as Data and the Theistic Likelihood
sections.rationale: The motion depends first on whether fine-tuning is an objective evidential datum and whether classical theism makes life-permitting conditions sufficiently expected.

sections.title: Scope and Granularity of the Comparison
sections.rationale: A comparative Bayesian inference requires a defined theistic hypothesis and a defined rival space whose members and level of specificity determine the relevant probabilities.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and Empirical Discrimination
sections.rationale: The force of fine-tuning evidence turns on whether available naturalistic auxiliaries legitimately diffuse the inference or instead generate unrestricted empirical skepticism.

sections.title: Agency, Motive, and Predictive Fit
sections.rationale: Evidence for intentional agency supports classical theism only if it also supplies justified information about the agent's goodness, purposes, and expected actions.

sections.title: Coherence, Modesty, and Intrinsic Probability
sections.rationale: The inference requires an account of how probability is distributed among perfect-being theism, limited alternatives, and naturalism augmented to predict fine-tuning.

sections.title: Parsimony and the Overall Probability Balance
sections.rationale: The motion-level conclusion requires integrating the claimed fine-tuning likelihood advantage with ontological parsimony and other theoretical virtues across the full comparison.

routes.description: Establish early individual and group appearance testimony, interpret it as bodily resurrection testimony, and compare resurrection with naturalistic alternatives under historical explanatory criteria.
routes.successCriteria: The reported death, appearances, conversions, bodily-resurrection belief, and resulting movement must be sufficiently supported and collectively better expected under resurrection than under the proposed natural explanations.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus rose and that resurrection explains the early Christian testimony more adequately than the available naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early, apostolically connected sources report appearances to individuals and groups.
Establish that the relevant testimony concerns Jesus's transformed physical body rather than visions alone.
Show that hallucination, contagion, legendary development, and related natural mechanisms do not adequately explain the reported evidence.
Apply explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of unsupported assumptions to the competing hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Integrate Jesus's prior claims, reported deeds, prediction, appearances, conversions, and the resulting movement into the comparison.
Preserve the historical usefulness of the Gospel core despite literary shaping and peripheral differences.

routes.description: Require evidence proportionate to resurrection's low background probability and explain the testimony through established psychological, social, and literary processes.
routes.successCriteria: The surviving testimony must remain insufficiently exceptional to overcome resurrection's prior burden while visions, social contagion, missing-body scenarios, and tradition development remain adequate natural possibilities.

motionBridge.description: Show that the early Christian testimony does not warrant resurrection over established natural classes of explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that an unprecedented divine resurrection requires exceptionally strong confirming evidence.
Explain individual and group appearance beliefs through culturally conditioned visions, suggestion, and charismatic contagion.
Show that the early epistolary evidence lacks the detail needed to establish shared encounters with a physical Jesus or verification of an empty grave.
Account for detailed resurrection narratives through legendary growth, redaction, literary imitation, and mythmaking.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that loss, removal, or nonverification of a body can accompany appearance beliefs without resurrection.
Compare the reported narrow appearance pattern with what a local visionary movement and a universally revealing deity would predict.

sections.title: Historical Method and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: The governing comparison depends on whether explanatory criteria can bracket resurrection's prior probability or whether its lack of established precedent imposes an exceptional evidential burden.

sections.title: Early Testimony and Bodily Resurrection
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether the earliest evidence reports apostolically connected encounters with a transformed physical Jesus or sparse and culturally conditioned visionary experiences.

sections.title: Psychological and Group-Appearance Mechanisms
sections.rationale: A principal clash concerns whether known psychological and social processes can generate the reported individual and group experiences and the ensuing bodily-resurrection belief.

sections.title: Cumulative Explanatory Comparison
sections.rationale: The central inference requires comparing how the resurrection and naturalistic routes account for the combined reports rather than treating each appearance, conversion, or missing-body claim in isolation.

sections.title: Gospel Literary and Historical Value
sections.rationale: The detailed bodily and empty-tomb narratives depend partly on whether Gospel composition and disagreement preserve a usable historical core or instead indicate literary and legendary development.

routes.description: Establish that early Christian sources report a transformed but physically continuous risen Jesus and that their cumulative historical provenance supports occurrence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony is historically usable, bodily in meaning, and better explained by Jesus having physically risen than by the proposed alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically grounded early testimony about Jesus after death to the conclusion that the body that died was raised in transformed physical continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and other early Christian testimony preserves resurrection claims sufficiently early and coherently to bear historical weight.
Show that spiritual and glorious body language denotes transformed embodiment rather than an immaterial survival or apparition.
Connect reported appearances and geographically dispersed early teaching to identifiable witnesses or apostolic transmission.
Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan analogues and account for costly early proclamation without dissolving it into ordinary legend.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use costly adherence and continued proclamation to support the sincerity and claimed eyewitness grounding of the resurrection belief.
Treat convergence among distinct early sources and communities as support for a common antecedent resurrection tradition.

routes.description: Withhold the bodily-resurrection conclusion by applying ordinary historical analogy and challenging the meaning, provenance, and independence of the Christian testimony.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources do not historically distinguish a bodily resurrection from spiritual interpretation, legendary transmission, inherited ideology, or comparable religious narratives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant inferring an actual bodily return from death under provisional, analogy-based historical inquiry.

centralBridges.description: Apply comparison with ordinary experience and ancient religious narratives when judging the probability of an extraordinary resurrection report.
Show that Pauline flesh, spirit, and spiritual-body language does not require physical continuity with Jesus's dead body.
Challenge the authorship, consistency, independence, and apostolic pedigree of the documents and transmission chains offered as evidence.
Provide nonmiraculous explanations for uniform belief, costly commitment, martyrdom traditions, and the movement's expansion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between divine ability to resurrect and historical evidence that a resurrection actually occurred.
Identify pre-Christian or ancient structural parallels that weaken an inference from narrative uniqueness to historical occurrence.

sections.title: Historical method and extraordinary-event inference
sections.rationale: The motion requires an inference from ancient reports to an extraordinary event, making the governing historical standard and the evidential role of early reports foundational to both routes.

sections.title: Meaning of bodily and spiritual resurrection language
sections.rationale: Whether the earliest resurrection language describes transformed physical continuity or an immaterial spiritual condition bears directly on the bodily qualification in the motion.

sections.title: Provenance and coherence of Pauline testimony
sections.rationale: Pauline material is among the earliest evidence invoked, so whether its received and revealed formulations are coherent materially affects the historical foundation of the resurrection claim.

sections.title: Chronology and relevance of pagan resurrection analogues
sections.rationale: The presence or absence of earlier comparable dying-and-rising traditions affects whether the Christian accounts are treated as historically distinctive testimony or as familiar religious narrative forms.

sections.title: Independence and reliability of apostolic transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of later Christian agreement depends on whether it preserves independently grounded apostolic information or merely repeats contested attributions and normative inherited teaching.

sections.title: Martyrdom, costly commitment, and movement growth
sections.rationale: Claims about suffering and expansion can support the sincerity or origins of resurrection belief only if their historical basis and explanatory connection to the event are established.

routes.description: Establish God as the better explanation of natural order, rational norms, moral obligation, purpose, and the central claims of Christian experience.
routes.successCriteria: Show that these features of reality are more adequately grounded in an eternal personal mind than in an exclusively natural reality.

motionBridge.description: Connect the combined explanatory case for a transcendent personal mind to the conclusion that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Show that cosmic order, origins, fine-tuning, or biological information warrant an inference to intelligence.
Show that mind-independent logic and mathematical intelligibility require grounding in a transcendent mind.
Show that objective human value and binding moral duties require a personal standard beyond society.
Connect the historical and self-sacrificial account of Jesus to the character of the proposed God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend abductive inference to intelligent causes as legitimate rather than excluded by methodological assumptions.
Explain how relationship with God supplies purpose and reasons for costly service to other people.

routes.description: Withhold belief in God by requiring publicly testable support and explaining the cited natural, rational, moral, and experiential phenomena without deity.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the affirmative inferences do not demonstrate God because natural accounts remain available and religious claims lack reliable verification.

motionBridge.description: Connect the failure of the offered evidence to satisfy the affirmative burden with nonacceptance of God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Require testable, publicly verifiable evidence capable of distinguishing a real deity from unsupported religious claims.
Show that natural inquiry and uncertain origin models do not require a supernatural designer.
Explain logical and mathematical relations through the properties of things without invoking a divine mind.
Ground moral judgment and cooperation in harm, empathy, trust, and social dependence without divine command.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that conflicting and psychologically fallible religious experiences cannot identify a uniquely true religion.
Keep the burden on the party asserting an additional supernatural reality rather than demanding its disproof.

sections.title: Evidence, Method, and the Burden of Belief
sections.rationale: The governing standard of evidence determines whether design and religious claims can support the motion and who must establish an additional supernatural reality.

sections.title: Design, Biological Complexity, and Cosmic Origins
sections.rationale: The inference from natural structure and origins to intelligence is a direct route to God's existence and a principal point of dispute between the sides.

sections.title: Logic, Mathematics, and Intelligibility
sections.rationale: Whether objective rational relations require a mind is an independent bridge from the intelligibility of reality to a transcendent personal source.

sections.title: Morality, Altruism, and Human Purpose
sections.rationale: The debate's moral route turns on whether objective duties and costly altruism require divine grounding or can arise from human social and moral capacities.

sections.title: Christian Claims and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: The motion also depends on whether specifically Christian claims and personal experience reliably identify God rather than culturally variable or psychological belief.

routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole fundamental ontology and explain objective order, individual perspectives, causality, and nonspatiotemporal structure as configurations of universal subjectivity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a consciousness-only ontology avoids emergence while accounting for empirical regularity, external reality, differentiated subjects, causal efficacy, and structured relations without fundamental spacetime.

motionBridge.description: Show that consciousness is a more parsimonious and explanatorily complete ontological foundation than non-conscious matter or neutral primitives.

centralBridges.description: Explain how an observer-independent and scientifically ordered world can consist of external mental states represented through perception.
Explain individual selves and experiences as differentiated modes or excitations of one universal subjectivity.
Ground causal regularity in intrinsic properties and interactions within a single mental ontology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect physics, neuroscience, altered experience, and consciousness theory to predictions or implications consistent with idealism.
Account for fundamental structure through semantic or cognitive relations that do not require spatial or temporal extension.

routes.description: Deny that failures of materialist emergence establish idealism by developing a neutral representational alternative and testing whether idealism explains structure, causality, and subjecthood.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if neutral representational processes avoid the hard problem while consciousness-first language fails to add necessary explanatory content concerning ordered structure, causal agents, or experience.

motionBridge.description: Show that avoiding matter-to-consciousness emergence does not require treating consciousness as the ontological foundation of reality.

centralBridges.description: Locate phenomenal character in representations without positing either separately existing physical objects or universal consciousness as substance.
Require an account of how representations, organism boundaries, and predictable order arise rather than merely labeling their inaccessible substrate mental.
Determine where causal efficacy resides when the ordinary personal self is constructed, unstable, or absent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish correlations or mappings involving integrated information from an explanation of why subjective experience exists.
Test whether theories framed through brains, fields, vibrations, or processes can accommodate experience without ordinary space and time.

sections.title: Ontological foundation and empirical warrant
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether consciousness is the most economical fundamental given and whether available empirical considerations distinguish that proposal from a neutral alternative.

sections.title: External reality and explanatory structure
sections.rationale: A consciousness-first ontology must preserve an observer-independent ordered world and specify how perception, organisms, and regularities arise within its single category.

sections.title: Representation, self-models, and experience
sections.rationale: The distribution of phenomenal character across representations and the status of the personal self determine whether neutral representation suffices or still presupposes consciousness.

sections.title: Integrated information and explanatory scope
sections.rationale: Integrated information bears on the persistence and causal role of experience, but its relevance depends on whether it supplies operational prediction, metaphysical explanation, or limited ontological implications.

sections.title: Subjecthood and the source of causality
sections.rationale: The ontology must identify the bearer and source of causal efficacy when personal selves are modeled as constructed and dream contents may arise without an experienced agent.

sections.title: Structure without fundamental spacetime
sections.rationale: The account of fundamental reality must preserve differentiation and meaningful structure even when ordinary spatial and temporal organization is absent or nonfundamental.
